claim: Plasmodium falciparum is a causative agent of human malaria.
source: Plasmodium falciparum is a causative agent of human malaria.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the organism causing malaria.

claim: Sixty percent of mRNAs from P. falciparum's extremely AT-rich (81%) genome harbor long polyadenosine (polyA) runs within their ORFs.
source: Sixty percent of mRNAs from its extremely AT-rich (81%) genome harbor long polyadenosine (polyA) runs within their ORFs, distinguishing the parasite from its hosts and other sequenced organisms.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's bioinformatic analysis.

claim: PolyA runs cause ribosome stalling and frameshifting in most organisms.
source: Recent studies indicate polyA runs cause ribosome stalling and frameshifting, triggering mRNA surveillance pathways and attenuating protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endogenous genes and reporter sequences containing long polyA runs are efficiently and accurately translated in P. falciparum cells.
source: We demonstrate that both endogenous genes and reporter sequences containing long polyA runs are efficiently and accurately translated in P. falciparum cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: PolyA runs do not elicit any response from No Go Decay (NGD) in P. falciparum.
source: We show that polyA runs do not elicit any response from No Go Decay (NGD) or result in the production of frameshifted proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: PolyA runs do not result in the production of frameshifted proteins in P. falciparum.
source: We show that polyA runs do not elicit any response from No Go Decay (NGD) or result in the production of frameshifted proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The response to polyA runs in P. falciparum is in stark contrast to what is observed in human cells or T. thermophila.
source: This is in stark contrast to what we observe in human cells or T. thermophila, an organism with similar AT-content.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Plasmodium cells evolved not to have a fully functional NGD pathway.
source: Finally, using stalling reporters we show that Plasmodium cells evolved not to have a fully functional NGD pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data with stalling reporters.

claim: P. falciparum is responsible for 90% of all malaria-associated deaths.
source: The complex life cycle of Plasmodium falciparum, responsible for 90% of all malaria-associated deaths, involves multiple stages in both the human and mosquito hosts.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Asexual replication during the intraerythrocytic development cycle (IDC) is tightly regulated over a 48 hr period.
source: Asexual replication during the intraerythrocytic development cycle (IDC) is tightly regulated over a 48 hr period, involving the expression of the majority of its genes (Gerald et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2017; Caro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A range of 16–32 daughter cells results from the IDC.
source: A range of 16–32 daughter cells results from the IDC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: Genes associated with cell cycle control, translation, RNA metabolism, protein folding, and drug resistance are more likely to be essential for parasites fitness and survival.
source: Recent saturation-level mutagenesis of the P. falciparum genome further emphasized and demonstrated that genes associated with cell cycle control, translation, RNA metabolism, protein folding, and drug resistance are more likely to be essential for parasites fitness and survival (Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: P. falciparum genome averages ~81% in overall AT content.
source: However, a faithful execution of these fundamental processes is challenged by the extremely AT-rich P. falciparum genome: averaging ~81% in overall AT content.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the genome composition.

claim: P. falciparum represents a unique case from other AT-rich organisms with relatively small difference in AT-richness between the non-coding and coding regions.
source: With a relatively small difference in AT-richness between the non-coding and coding regions; P. falciparum represents a unique case from other AT-rich organisms (Glöckner, 2000; Szafranski et al., 2005; Zilversmit et al., 2010; Erath et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presence of just 12 adenosines in an mRNA-coding region was found to reduce the yield of protein synthesis by more than 40% in human tissue cultures.
source: In human tissue cultures, the presence of just 12 adenosines in an mRNA-coding region was found to reduce the yield of protein synthesis by more than 40%, and runs of 30–60 adenosine nucleotides reduce protein synthesis by more than 90% (Arthur et al., 2015; Arthur et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Runs of 30–60 adenosine nucleotides reduce protein synthesis by more than 90% in human tissue cultures.
source: In human tissue cultures, the presence of just 12 adenosines in an mRNA-coding region was found to reduce the yield of protein synthesis by more than 40%, and runs of 30–60 adenosine nucleotides reduce protein synthesis by more than 90% (Arthur et al., 2015; Arthur et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effect of polyA tracts on translation was observed in all tested organisms including fruit flies, yeasts, plants and E. coli.
source: This effect on translation was observed in all tested organisms that include fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster), yeasts (Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans), plants (Arabidopsis thaliana, and Nicotiana benthamiana) and E. coli (Zilversmit et al., 2010; Arthur et al., 2015; Koutmou et al., 2015; Tournu et al., 2019; Szádeczky-Kardoss et al., 2018; Tuck et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High AU-content within transcript coding regions and an extreme AAA and AAU codon bias increase the propensity for polyA tracts in the P. falciparum transcriptome.
source: High AU-content within transcript coding regions and an extreme AAA and AAU codon bias increase the propensity for polyA tracts in the P. falciparum transcriptome (Saul and Battistutta, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: P. falciparum has a 'just-in-time' transcriptional and translational model of gene expression during the trophozoite stage.
source: Additionally, a 'just-in-time' transcriptional and translational model of gene expression during the relatively short trophozoite stage of the P. falciparum IDC (Lu et al., 2017; Coulson et al., 2004) make a rapid protein synthesis in an AU-rich transcriptome an appealing problem.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: P. falciparum and other members of the Plasmodium genus have a much higher ratio of polyA tract genes when normalized to genomic AT-content compared to other eukaryotic organisms.
source: Analyses of the selected set of eukaryotic genomes indicate that P. falciparum and other members of the Plasmodium genus have a much higher ratio of polyA tract genes when normalized to genomic AT-content (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The feature of high polyA tract genes in Plasmodium species is conserved regardless of their genomic AT-content.
source: Interestingly, this feature of Plasmodium species is conserved regardless of their genomic AT-content, resulting in two groups (low and high AT-content Plasmodium spp.) with unusually large portions of polyA tract genes ranging from 35 to over 65% of the total transcriptome (Figure 1A; Erath et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Over 63% of genes in P. falciparum have polyA tract motifs.
source: Over 63% of genes in P. falciparum have polyA tract motifs, while only 0.7–2% of total genes in humans and mosquito genomes, respectively, contain these motifs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Only 0.7–2% of total genes in humans and mosquito genomes contain polyA tract motifs.
source: Over 63% of genes in P. falciparum have polyA tract motifs, while only 0.7–2% of total genes in humans and mosquito genomes, respectively, contain these motifs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The P. falciparum 3D7 genome contains 188 genes with 16 consecutive adenosines.
source: The P. falciparum 3D7 genome contains 188 genes with 16As, while the human host and AT-rich T. thermophila together have only three genes (T. thermophila two and H. sapiens 1) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: T. thermophila had almost nine times less genes with twelve consecutive adenosines than P. falciparum.
source: Additionally, T. thermophila a protozoan with an overall 73% AT-rich genome and 24,000 predicted genes, had almost nine times less genes with twelve consecutive adenosines than P. falciparum, 172 and 1526, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Ensembl database reports 105 P. falciparum 3D7 genes with exactly 18As and more than 150 genes with more than 20 consecutive adenosines.
source: Ensembl database reports 105 P. falciparum 3D7 genes with exactly 18As and more than 150 genes with more than 20 consecutive adenosines (20-65As, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from database analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PlasmoDB reports 329 P. falciparum genes having runs of ≥20 consecutive adenosines.
source: Analyses of P. falciparum genomes in the PlasmoDB database (Beznosková et al., 2013), curated explicitly for malaria parasite species, report more than double that number with 329 genes having runs of ≥20 consecutive adenosines.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from database analysis.

claim: The maximum length of consecutive adenosine runs in coding sequences of Plasmodium genomes is 111 As in P. falciparum fch four strain.
source: Finally, the maximum length of consecutive adenosine runs in coding sequences of Plasmodium genomes indicated 111 As in P. falciparum fch four strain with the human host or 132 As in P. reichenowi, strain causing chimpanzee malaria (Erath et al., 2019; Habich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from database analysis supported by citations.

claim: The length of polyA runs in coding sequences of malaria parasites exceeds the length of the average size of 3'UTR polyA tails found on the majority of transcripts in eukaryotic species.
source: As such, the length of polyA runs in coding sequences of malaria parasites exceeds the length of the average size of 3'UTR polyA tails found on the majority of transcripts in eukaryotic species (Subtelny et al., 2014; Brown and Sachs, 1998; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative finding supported by citations.

claim: P. falciparum had the highest abundance of transcripts hosting four consecutive AAA codons in runs of four lysine residues.
source: P. falciparum had the highest abundance of transcripts hosting four consecutive AAA codons in runs of four lysine residues (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 70–85% of orthologs of polyA tract carrying genes from P. falciparum have the same polyA motifs in genes from other Plasmodium species.
source: Previous analysis indicated that 70–85% of orthologs of polyA tract carrying genes from P. falciparum have the same polyA motifs in genes from other Plasmodium species, regardless of their genomic AT content (Habich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A majority of Plasmodium polyA tracts genes and poly-lysine proteins fall into the group of essential genes.
source: A majority of Plasmodium polyA tracts genes and poly-lysine proteins fall into the group of essential genes based on the recent mutagenesis studies (Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Gene ontology results indicate enrichment in gene products involved in crucial cellular processes such as protein synthesis, RNA biogenesis, and chromosome segregation.
source: This outcome is expected given that gene ontology results indicate enrichment in gene products involved in crucial cellular processes such as protein synthesis, RNA biogenesis, and chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis.

claim: Plasmodium species had enrichment of polyA tract motifs in a group of genes defined as the cellular and pathological cell adhesion ontology group.
source: In addition to these groups, Plasmodium species also had enrichment of polyA tract motifs in a group of genes defined as the cellular and pathological cell adhesion ontology group (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from gene ontology analysis.

claim: Insertion of the 36 adenosine nucleotide (36 As) resulted in robust changes in normalized mRNA levels in HDFs and T. thermophila.
source: We observed robust changes in normalized mRNA levels (Figure 2A) and substantial losses in protein expression (Figure 2B) for reporters with polyA tracts (+polyA36) in both HDFs and AT-rich T. thermophila (Arthur et al., 2017; Arthur and Djuranovic, 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Insertion of the 36 adenosine nucleotide (36 As) resulted in substantial losses in protein expression in HDFs and T. thermophila.
source: We observed robust changes in normalized mRNA levels (Figure 2A) and substantial losses in protein expression (Figure 2B) for reporters with polyA tracts (+polyA36) in both HDFs and AT-rich T. thermophila (Arthur et al., 2017; Arthur and Djuranovic, 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Minimal, if any, effects from polyA tract insertion on reporter mRNA and protein expression were observed in P. falciparum cells.
source: In comparison to HDFs and T. thermophila, we observed minimal, if any, effects from polyA tract insertion on reporter mRNA and protein expression in P. falciparum cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Live-fluorescence microscopy confirms the equivalent expression of mCherry reporter between constructs with and without polyA tract in P. falciparum.
source: Further analysis of P. falciparum cells by live-fluorescence microscopy confirms the equivalent expression of mCherry reporter, judging by the intensity of fluorescence between constructs with and without polyA tract (+polyA36 and –polyA36, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Measurement of nanoluc luminescence indicates similar expression of a reporter with a polyA tract (+polyA36) compared with the control reporter (-polyA36) in P. falciparum.
source: Measurement of nanoluc luminescence from the same number of drug-selected parasites indicates similar expression of a reporter with a polyA tract (+polyA36) compared with the control reporter (-polyA36, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Western blot analyses of nanoluc reporters did not indicate the HA-tagged protein band at 14kD that would represent frameshifted nanoluc.
source: Western blot analyses of nanoluc reporters did not indicate the HA-tagged protein band at 14kD that would represent frameshifted nanoluc (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of mCherry reporters showed only equivalent amounts of the full-length product.
source: Moreover, the immunoprecipitation of mCherry reporters showed only equivalent amounts of the full-length product (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: 2D PAGE electrophoresis indicated a shift in isoelectric point (pI) of approximately one pH unit for the (+polyA36) construct compared to the wild-type one (-polyA36).
source: This analysis indicated a shift in isoelectric point (pI) of approximately one pH unit for the (+polyA36) construct compared to the wild-type one (-polyA36), 7.2–7.4 and 6.25–6.5, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 2D PAGE analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The shift on the 2D PAGE gels was the same for construct with 12xAAG lysine codons and is expected based on the calculated isoelectric points if all 12xAAA or 12xAAG codons were translated into lysine residues.
source: This shift on the 2D PAGE gels was the same for construct with 12xAAG lysine codons and is expected based on the calculated isoelectric points if all 12xAAA or 12xAAG codons were translated into lysine residues.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the 2D PAGE analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cumulative data for all transcripts with polyA tracts from human cells indicate substantial translational pausing on these sequences.
source: Cumulative data for all transcripts with polyA tracts from human cells indicate substantial translational pausing on these sequences (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Analyses of P. falciparum ribosome profiling dataset indicated no evidence for ribosome stalling in P. falciparum transcripts containing polyA tracts.
source: However, analyses of previously published P. falciparum ribosome profiling dataset (Caro et al., 2014) indicated no evidence for ribosome stalling in P. falciparum transcripts containing polyA tracts.
evidence: This is a finding from ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: Normalized ribosome occupancy for P. falciparum transcripts with a length of less than or equal to 22 consecutive adenosine nucleotides indicated more or less equal ribosome occupancy over polyA tract.
source: Normalized ribosome occupancy for P. falciparum transcripts with a length of less than or equal to 22 consecutive adenosine nucleotides (≤22As), that code for more than seven consecutive lysines, indicated more or less equal ribosome occupancy over polyA tract (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The translation of endogenous polyA tracts is independent of different stages of P. falciparum IDC.
source: We found that the translation of endogenous polyA tracts is independent of different stages of P. falciparum IDC, as we did not notice any significant difference in the distribution of ribosome protected fragments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a finding from ribosome profiling data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A time-course study of synchronized parasite culture indicated that the selected polyA tract transcripts are efficiently transcribed at all-time points when compared to the control gene.
source: A time-course study of synchronized parasite culture indicated that the selected polyA tract transcripts are efficiently transcribed at all-time points when compared to the control gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the qRT-PCR time-course experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The coding sequences from T. thermophila and P. falciparum yielded structures with higher predicted minimum free energy (MFE) than those from the coding sequences of human genes.
source: On average, the coding sequences from T. thermophila and P. falciparum yielded structures with higher predicted minimum free energy (MFE; Figure 4—figure supplement 5), than those from the coding sequences of human genes
evidence: This is a finding from the in silico RNA structure analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Transcriptome z-scores revealed no significant differences between P. falciparum and T. thermophila.
source: Interestingly transcriptome z-scores revealed no significant differences between P. falciparum and T. thermophila (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the in silico RNA structure analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: P. falciparum coding sequences do not appear ordered to adopt structures any more stable than would be expected for random sequences or with the same nucleotide content found in T. thermophila.
source: This suggests that globally, P. falciparum coding sequences do not appear ordered to adopt structures any more stable than would be expected for random sequences or with the same nucleotide content found in T. thermophila.
evidence: This is an inference from the in silico RNA structure analysis.

claim: The bioinformatics search of the P. falciparum genome did not identify an apparent homolog of Hbs1.
source: Our bioinformatics search of the P. falciparum genome did not identify an apparent homolog of Hbs1 nor the recently reported S. cerevisiae endonuclease Cue2 (NONU-1 in C. elegans) (D'Orazio et al., 2019; Glover, 2019; Navickas, 2019) in P. falciparum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The bioinformatics search of the P. falciparum genome did not identify an apparent homolog of the S. cerevisiae endonuclease Cue2.
source: Our bioinformatics search of the P. falciparum genome did not identify an apparent homolog of Hbs1 nor the recently reported S. cerevisiae endonuclease Cue2 (NONU-1 in C. elegans) (D'Orazio et al., 2019; Glover, 2019; Navickas, 2019) in P. falciparum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Insertion of the RNA stem-loop resulted in a severe reduction of reporter protein levels in P. falciparum.
source: Insertion of the RNA stem-loop resulted in a severe reduction of reporter protein levels (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), but moderate increase in mRNA levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Insertion of the RNA stem-loop resulted in a moderate increase in mRNA levels in P. falciparum.
source: Insertion of the RNA stem-loop resulted in a severe reduction of reporter protein levels (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), but moderate increase in mRNA levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Polysome profile analyses indicated that mRNA of StL construct was associated mostly with polysome fractions 7–9 that correspond to the disome peak.
source: Polysome profile analyses indicated that mRNA of StL construct was associated mostly with polysome fractions 7–9 that correspond to the disome peak.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the polysome profiling experiment shown in Figure 5C.

claim: mRNAs for constructs with and without polyA tracts (±polyA36) and for PfGAPDH were distributed more evenly along the polysome fractions.
source: mRNAs for constructs with and without polyA tracts (±polyA36) and for PfGAPDH were distributed more evenly along the polysome fractions (fractions 9–16).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the polysome profiling experiment shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Stable RNA structures in mRNAs stall P. falciparum ribosomes, reducing protein synthesis from such transcript, however without significant impact on mRNA stability.
source: These experiments argue that stable RNA structures in mRNAs stall P. falciparum ribosomes, reducing protein synthesis from such transcript, however without significant impact on mRNA stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data with the stem-loop construct.

claim: The mRNA and protein levels of PfPelo were moderately increased (approximately two-fold) in response to the Ile-starvation.
source: The mRNA and protein levels of PfPelo were moderately increased (approximately two-fold), while levels of PfHsp70 were strongly induced (five-fold increase) in response to the Ile-starvation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Ile-starvation experiment shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Levels of PfHsp70 were strongly induced (five-fold increase) in response to the Ile-starvation.
source: The mRNA and protein levels of PfPelo were moderately increased (approximately two-fold), while levels of PfHsp70 were strongly induced (five-fold increase) in response to the Ile-starvation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Ile-starvation experiment shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: No overall change in mRNA stability is observed for Ile-rich P. falciparum genes during Ile-starvation.
source: We did not observe the general reduction in mRNA levels for Ile-rich P. falciparum genes when we compared starved to non-starved control samples. We, instead found a slight increase in mRNA abundance for several Ile-rich transcripts during starvation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Ile-starvation experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A slight increase in mRNA abundance for several Ile-rich transcripts was found during starvation.
source: We did not observe the general reduction in mRNA levels for Ile-rich P. falciparum genes when we compared starved to non-starved control samples. We, instead found a slight increase in mRNA abundance for several Ile-rich transcripts during starvation (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Ile-starvation experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both increase in expression of NGD-associated factor, Pelota, and protein chaperone HSP70 may contribute to cell survival, ribosome recycling and mRNA stabilization during amino acid starvation in P. falciparum.
source: However, our result indicated that both increase in expression of NGD-associated factor, Pelota, and protein chaperone HSP70 may contribute to cell survival, ribosome recycling and mRNA stabilization during amino acid starvation in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is an inference from the Ile-starvation experimental data.

claim: RQC and NGD pathway in P. falciparum cells are not connected, at least directly, to targeted mRNA degradation.
source: These results may indicate that RQC and NGD pathway in P. falciparum cells are not connected, at least directly, to targeted mRNA degradation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The ribosome exit tunnel of P. falciparum seems to be generally more hydrophilic, including the constriction site.
source: Along this line, the ribosome exit tunnel of P. falciparum seems to be generally more hydrophilic, including the constriction site.
evidence: This is a finding from the structural analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The ribosome peptide exit tunnel of parasites adapted to accommodate synthesis of long runs of poly-lysine residues by reducing electrostatic barriers below the PTC and at the constriction site.
source: Taken together, it seems that the ribosome peptide exit tunnel of parasites adapted to accommodate synthesis of long runs of poly-lysine residues by reducing electrostatic barriers below the PTC and at the constriction site.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: Runs of lysine and arginine residues are underrepresented in the proteome of multiple organisms compared to the runs of other amino acids.
source: Runs of lysine and arginine residues are underrepresented in the proteome of multiple organisms compared to the runs of other amino acids, suggesting a selective pressure against polybasic amino acid sequences (Karlin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Runs of lysine AAA codons exhibit a more significant delay in ribosome movement than an equivalent number of AAG lysine codons.
source: However, multiple biochemical analyses of poly-lysine stalling sequences, in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems, revealed that runs of lysine AAA codons exhibit a more significant delay in ribosome movement than an equivalent number of AAG lysine codons (Glöckner, 2000; Szafranski et al., 2005; Zilversmit et al., 2010; Arthur et al., 2015; Koutmou et al., 2015; Tournu et al., 2019; Szádeczky-Kardoss et al., 2018; Chandrasekaran et al., 2019; Tuck et al., 2020; Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endogenous sites with 8–9 As are sufficient to cause recruitment of mRNA surveillance pathways in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: More recent study in mouse embryonic stem cells indicates that besides 12A-1 sequences endogenous sites with 8–9 As are sufficient to cause recruitment of mRNA surveillance pathways (Tuck et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ribosome stalling and frameshifting induced by polyA runs depend on the sequence and conformation of the mRNA in the ribosome, with a questionable contribution by the nascent polypeptide chain.
source: However, ribosome stalling and frameshifting induced by polyA runs depend on the sequence and conformation of the mRNA in the ribosome, with a questionable contribution by the nascent polypeptide chain (Arthur et al., 2015; Arthur and Djuranovic, 2018; Koutmou et al., 2015; Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The atypical enrichment in polyA tracts in the coding sequence of mRNAs is a feature that is conserved in most Plasmodium species.
source: The atypical enrichment in polyA tracts in the coding sequence of mRNAs, translated into long poly-lysine runs in proteins, is a feature that is conserved in most Plasmodium species (Figure 1; Caro et al., 2014; Habich et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015; Aurrecoechea et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The increased AT-richness and number of polyA tracts in P. falciparum could be a result of selective pressure on biosynthetic pathways and the oxidative intraerythrocytic environment.
source: The increased AT-richness and number of polyA tracts in P. falciparum, as such, could be a result of selective pressure on biosynthetic pathways (AT vs. GC biosynthesis) (Seward and Kelly, 2016; Dietel et al., 2019) and the oxidative intraerythrocytic environment (Becker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Advantages for the parasites to synthesize proteins with poly-lysine repeats could be solely driven by benefits in the adhesion and invasion of host cells or export of numerous parasite proteins to the surface of infected erythrocytes.
source: It is attractive to speculate that advantages for the parasites to synthesize proteins with poly-lysine repeats could be solely driven by benefits in the adhesion and invasion of host cells (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Leitgeb et al., 2011) or export of numerous parasite proteins to the surface of infected erythrocytes (Davies et al., 2016; Romero et al., 2004; Hancock et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The change in nucleotide composition and a number of long polyA tracts of P. falciparum probably shaped NGD/NSD mRNA surveillance responses in parasites.
source: However, the change in nucleotide composition and a number of long polyA tracts of P. falciparum (Figure 1) probably shaped NGD/NSD mRNA surveillance responses in parasites (seen in Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 1, 5, and 6.

claim: The loss of Cue2/Nonu-1 in Plasmodium cells can not completely explain the lack of mRNA degradation on the stem-loop construct or in Ile-starvation experiments.
source: However, the loss of Cue2/Nonu-1 in Plasmodium cells can not completely explain the lack of mRNA degradation on the stem-loop construct (Figure 5) or in Ile-starvation experiments (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: P. falciparum ribosomes had to change to accommodate correct and efficient protein synthesis from the runs of coding polyA tracts that are longer than the average size of 3'-UTR polyA tails in other organisms.
source: Unambiguously, P. falciparum ribosomes had to change to accommodate correct and efficient protein synthesis from the runs of coding polyA tracts that are longer than the average size of 3'-UTR polyA tails in other organisms (Subtelny et al., 2014; Brown and Sachs, 1998; Chang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The fact that Plasmodium ribosome lacks interaction with PfRACK1 protein could be beneficial for the translation of polyA tracts into poly-lysine runs.
source: The fact that recent cryo-EM structures indicated that the Plasmodium ribosome lacks interaction with PfRACK1 protein (Figure 7) could be beneficial for the translation of polyA tracts into poly-lysine runs (Wong et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural data and citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible to speculate that P. falciparum specific ribosome extension segments in the 40S subunit may have the role in recruiting other Plasmodium proteins that may help with translation of polyA tracts and poly-lysine repeats.
source: It is possible to speculate that P. falciparum specific ribosome extension segments in the 40S subunit may have the role in recruiting other Plasmodium proteins that may help with translation of polyA tracts and poly-lysine repeats (Wong et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An inhibitory conformation of mRNA in the A-site of the ribosome, as well as the polybasic character of the nascent polypeptide chain in the ribosome peptide exit tunnel, are crucial for the poly(A)-mediated stalling mechanism.
source: However, it was recently indicated that an inhibitory conformation of mRNA in the A-site of the ribosome, as well as the polybasic character of the nascent polypeptide chain in the ribosome, peptide exit tunnel, are crucial for the poly(A)-mediated stalling mechanism (Chandrasekaran et al., 2019; Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in the peptide exit tunnel of P. falciparum ribosomes might have partially contributed to the adaptation to the synthesis of long poly-lysine runs by reducing the potential stalling effects associated with translocation of polybasic peptides through hydrophobic environment.
source: It might be that changes in the peptide exit tunnel of P. falciparum ribosomes (Figure 7) have partially contributed to the adaptation to the synthesis of long poly-lysine runs by reducing the potential stalling effects associated with translocation of polybasic peptides through hydrophobic environment (Fujita et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural data and citations to previous research.

claim: To adapt to polyA tract translation for the production of the polybasic and homopolymeric lysine repeats, the malaria-causing parasite has altered its mRNA translation quality control pathways as well as its ribosomal proteins and ribosome structure.
source: In conclusion, to adapt to polyA tract translation for the production of the polybasic and homopolymeric lysine repeats, the malaria-causing parasite has altered its mRNA translation quality control pathways as well as its ribosomal proteins and ribosome structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The additional diversity of Plasmodium spp. rRNAs and possible activity of yet unknown ribosome-associated factors promote the possibility of Plasmodium 'specialized ribosomes,' which allow for polyA tract translation into poly-lysine sequences of functional proteins.
source: The additional diversity of Plasmodium spp. rRNAs (Walliker et al., 1987; McCutchan et al., 1988; Waters et al., 1989) and possible activity of yet unknown ribosome-associated factors promote the possibility of Plasmodium 'specialized ribosomes,' which allow for polyA tract translation into poly-lysine sequences of functional proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: P. falciparum and other members of the Plasmodium genus distinguish themselves from their hosts and other sequenced organisms by harboring long polyadenosine runs within their ORFs.
source: Sixty percent of mRNAs from its extremely AT-rich (81%) genome harbor long polyadenosine (polyA) runs within their ORFs, distinguishing the parasite from its hosts and other sequenced organisms.
evidence: This is an implicit claim that Plasmodium is unique in this feature compared to other organisms.

claim: The majority of P. falciparum 28S associated rRNA expansion segments (ESs) are shorter than in human rRNA.
source: While the majority of P. falciparum 28S associated rRNA expansion segments (ESs) are shorter than in human rRNA, 18S ESs are generally larger (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 18S ESs in P. falciparum are generally larger than in human rRNA.
source: While the majority of P. falciparum 28S associated rRNA expansion segments (ESs) are shorter than in human rRNA, 18S ESs are generally larger (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of RACK1 protein on Plasmodium ribosomes could be the most prominent features regarding the translation of polyA tracts and poly-lysine repeats.
source: On the other hand, while being essential and one of the most well-expressed proteins in P. falciparum cells (Wang et al., 2015; Blomqvist et al., 2017), the absence of RACK1 protein on Plasmodium ribosomes could be the most prominent features regarding the translation of polyA tracts and poly-lysine repeats (Wong et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2015; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural data and citations to previous research.

claim: The deletion of RACK1/Asc1 in human or yeast cells was shown to increase the production of proteins with polybasic peptides, however, at the cost of increased frameshifting.
source: The deletion of RACK1/Asc1 in human or yeast cells was also shown to increase the production of proteins with polybasic peptides, however, at the cost of increased frameshifting (Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017; Kuroha et al., 2010; Wolf and Grayhack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The absence of Asc1 in yeast generally slows down elongation, promoting frameshifting on problematic CGA-CGA pairs.
source: The recent report has shown that the absence of Asc1 in yeast generally slows down elongation, promoting frameshifting on problematic CGA-CGA pairs (Tesina et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The proposed mechanism for polyA stalling induction should not depend on species, because ribosome nucleotides interacting with π-stacked polyA sequences are universally conserved.
source: This proposed mechanism for polyA stalling induction should not depend on species, because ribosome nucleotides interacting with π-stacked polyA sequences are universally conserved (A1756 and C1634, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.
